I explain how the loophole arises naturally from consideration of relevant symmetry transformations, and then I appeal to the partial/complete observables formalism to argue that the same loophole will work for any type of Wigner's Friend experiment, even if it is performed with a variable that does not obviously look like it requires relativization to a reference system. Finally I compare the loophole to other possible responses to the Local Friendliness theorem, and I show that the same loophole will work for other Extended Wigner's Friend theorems too.

papers.title: Chirality-Induced Angular-Momentum Pumping by Moving Charges
papers.authors: Jun-ichiro Kishine; Ron Naaman
papers.abstract: Chirality-induced spin selectivity is established even in light elements at room temperature; dissipation and electron correlations are implicated, here combined in one mechanism. Injected electron wave packets coherently radiate chiral phonons; electronic absorption competing with phonon decay sets the fraction electrons receive and its temperature dependence. Spin-orbit coupling itself is not renormalized; it becomes effectively large because both the orbital and spin moments it couples are enhanced by Coulomb correlations.

papers.title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
papers.authors: Jixuan Ruan; Zhuo Cui; Zhengding Hu; Zhongkai Yu; Xiang Fang; Yue Guan; Jason Ludmir; Phillip E. Weinberg; Xiuzhe Luo; Shengtao Wang; Sonia Lopez Alarcon; Hezi Zhang; Yufei Ding
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.

papers.title: Lieb-Robinson bounds for Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians via path expansions
papers.authors: Alexander Elgart; Marius Lemm
papers.abstract: We study the transport properties of Bose-Hubbard-type Hamiltonians. Kuwahara, Vu, and Saito proved sharp bounds on (i) particle transport and (ii) the Lieb-Robinson velocity for initial states with controlled boson density. We provide simpler and shorter proofs for both results using a new set of methods. For (i), boson transport, we use a class of weighted extended particle number operators that directly enables closing the associated differential inequalities. For (ii), the Lieb-Robinson bounds, we develop a bosonic version of the Chen-Lucas path expansion technique and recover the sharp velocity bound $t^{d-1}$ up to logarithmic corrections, where $d$ denotes the lattice dimension. We also extend the transport bounds (i) to long-range hopping with a power-law exponent $α>d$. The range $α\in (d,d+1)$ corresponds to an algebraic light cone for boson transport and has not been previously covered.

papers.title: Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem
papers.authors: Dingqian Wang; Jiayi Zhao; Ge Bai
papers.abstract: Experiments on a multi-time quantum process may reveal its responses only on selected, possibly overlapping, sets of times. We ask whether these partial descriptions admit a common underlying process, and formulate this process tensor marginal problem as a semidefinite feasibility test. Agreement on overlaps is necessary but insufficient: three locally consistent qubit marginals can have no common extension. Another family is incompatible as a time-ordered process even though a single quantum channel satisfies both its channel and temporal marginal constraints. This isolates temporal causality as the obstruction. We quantify incompatibility by the mixing needed to restore compatibility and derive finite tests using separate interventions at each time and final measurements. We further show that incompatibility is equivalent to an advantage over every compatible family in a multi-time process-discrimination task. Together, these results test whether process descriptions obtained in different experiments can arise from one causally ordered quantum process.

papers.title: What is the connection between quantum relationality and symmetry-based relationality?
papers.authors: Emily Adlam
papers.abstract: Although it has often been noted that both quantum mechanics and relativistic physics involve significant forms of relationality, the nature of the connection remains unclear. In addressing such a question it makes sense to start from the simplest possibility, so in this article I set out to consider the viability of the hypothesis that the two types of relationality are ultimately the same: that is, quantum states always characterize degrees of freedom which can be changed by a symmetry transformation, so they are relativized for exactly the same reason as partial observables in general relativity. I use the idea that we only measure partial observables to argue that this suggestion is compatible with all existing empirical evidence for quantum mechanics, and then I consider the consequences for ongoing debates about the nature of measurement in quantum mechanics.

papers.title: From Fabrication Disorder to Quantum-Protocol Yield in Inverse-Designed Silicon Photonic Beam Splitters
papers.authors: Nail Letty; Tahmeed Ul Islam; Wayesh Qarony
papers.abstract: Telecom-band silicon spin-photon qubits offer a promising platform for scalable quantum networks and distributed information processing, but their fixed emission wavelengths require compact, low-loss beam splitters with precise splitting and fabrication robustness. Conventional designs can face trade-offs between footprint, optical performance, and wavelength-specific operation. Here, we employ adjoint-based inverse design to optimize photonic geometries beyond conventional layouts, developing 1*2 Y-splitters and 2*2 directional couplers for the silicon T (1326 nm) and Al1 (1482.44 nm) spin-photon qubits. The devices achieve footprints of 2.9 and 26 um^2, respectively, with excess losses of 0.14-0.44 dB and back-reflection below 5*10^-4. We assess fabrication tolerance using 100-realization Monte Carlo simulations incorporating etch bias, line-edge roughness, thickness, and refractive-index variations. Mirror symmetry reduces the splitting-ratio spread of the Y-splitter by a factor of seven to nine relative to the directional coupler. We translate these variations into dual-rail fidelity, ideal splitting-ratio-limited Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. All realizations satisfy a protocol-performance threshold of 0.95. At 0.99, the tolerated splitting-ratio deviation shrinks from 0.035 for visibility to 0.0035 for min-entropy, and the simulated yields are 68% (T) and 91% (Al1) for coupler visibility and 90% (T) and 66% (Al1) for Y-splitter min-entropy. The tolerance of the target protocol, rather than the device alone, therefore sets the fabrication requirement for silicon spin-photon beam splitters.

papers.title: Sound-wave interference reveals the symmetry of a quantum transition
papers.authors: Sergei Studenikin; Yousef Karimi Yonjali; Alex Bogan; Andy Sachrajda; Shabir Barzanjeh
papers.abstract: A single sound quantum emitted from two places interferes with itself, like a particle passing through two slits. The fringe position reveals whether the sources emit with the same sign (symmetric) or opposite signs (antisymmetric). Knowing this symmetry is important because qubits in solids lose energy by emitting such sound quanta, phonons. For a qubit shared between two sites, antisymmetric emission cancels at long wavelengths, suppressing energy loss, whereas symmetric emission does not. Lifetime measurements give only the total loss and cannot distinguish them. Such fringes appear in double quantum dots, but their position has not been analysed. Here we measure it for single phonons emitted as one hole tunnels between two gallium arsenide quantum dots. Using a quantitative model of sound focusing in the crystal, we find that the two dots emit antisymmetrically, as expected for a moving charge, with only a small symmetric part. Spin-flip transitions in a magnetic field weaken the fringes without shifting them. For double-dot charge qubits, antisymmetric emission is predicted to reduce phonon losses strongly at the frequencies where qubits operate, and phonon interferometry gives a direct way to measure how qubits release energy and to design longer-lived qubits.

papers.title: Classical and Quantum Dynamics in State Space: Projective Hilbert Space, Measurement, and Classical Emergence
papers.authors: Alexey A. Kryukov
papers.abstract: We develop a geometric formulation of classical and quantum dynamics in which projective Hilbert space is taken as the primary state space and classical configuration and phase spaces arise as submanifolds of localized quantum states. The Fubini-Study metric induces the Euclidean metric on these submanifolds, while the tangential component of Schrödinger evolution reproduces Hamiltonian and Newtonian dynamics. We then extend the construction to stochastic motion. Brownian dynamics on the localized classical manifold is lifted to a common stochastic unitary evolution in projective Hilbert space; under homogeneity, isotropy, and independence assumptions, the corresponding Hermitian increments have Gaussian Unitary Ensemble statistics. This yields a random-matrix Schrödinger dynamics whose transition probabilities depend only on Fubini-Study distance. Through the embedding of localized states, the classical Gaussian transition law becomes the Born rule in projective state space. Measurement outcomes are identified with first arrival at detector-defined finite-resolution equivalence classes, while each realized state-space evolution remains linear and unitary. The framework is applied to classical emergence, macroscopic stabilization, double-slit experiments, composite systems, and entangled states. A spatially local Caldeira-Leggett-type system-environment model is also shown, under explicit thermal, symmetry, Ohmic, and coarse-graining assumptions, to generate the Brownian family required by the stochastic lift. The remaining open problem is to establish the range and universality of this mechanism for realistic many-body measuring environments.

papers.title: Detection times are not local observables in quantum field theory
papers.authors: Charis Anastopoulos; Ntina Savvidou
papers.abstract: Detection times are routinely recorded in quantum experiments. We show that, under natural covariance and consistency requirements, the observables describing these times cannot be algebraically localized in any bounded spacetime region, even when the records themselves are localized. This challenges the identification of algebraic localization with the physical localization of measurements and shows why microcausality alone does not establish non-signalling for measurements in quantum field theory.

papers.title: Interaction order sets the onset cost of steady-state quantum magic
papers.authors: Mingdi Xu
papers.abstract: Maintaining quantum magic under continuous noise requires coherent control and a supply of purity. We determine the cost of local stabilizer replacement resets sustaining any positive stationary magic in autonomous qubit networks with depolarization rate $γ$, interactions on at most $k$ sites, and Hamiltonian strength $J$ per site. An exact global stabilizer decomposition and a matching finite construction give the optimal onset scaling $γ(γ/J)^{1/(k-1)}$, uniformly over network size and noisy ancillas. For two-body interactions, the leading maximal-reset-rate coefficient is $1/(2\sqrt2)$ for every fixed finite size $N\ge2$, allowing mixed reset targets and heterogeneous rates. The same coefficient holds uniformly over growing networks with pure Pauli targets and equal reset rates. The converse combines hafnian stabilizer geometry with a positive random-order forest expansion.

papers.title: Classical and Quantum Logics with Multiple Non-Equivalent and Non-Isomorphic Models
papers.authors: Mladen Pavicic
papers.abstract: Both quantum and classical logics have several mutually non-equivalent and non-isomorphic models as has repeatedly been proved in the literature. Yet, several authors have recently come with criticisms of this result. In this paper, we show that the criticisms are either unfounded or wrong.

papers.title: Rule-based hardware-configurable static analysis for quantum programs
papers.authors: Yi-Ting Chen; Lauren Capelluto; Ryan Shaffer; Jeffrey Heckey
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of quantum hardware necessitates an adaptable static analysis framework for validating quantum programs. In this work, we introduce SHARP, a rule-based static analysis framework designed for OpenQASM that decouples hardware-specific constraints from the validation engine. By employing a rule-based approach, SHARP allows quantum computing services to validate programs against evolving instruction set architectures (ISAs) without having to modify the core analysis engine. SHARP achieves this by ingesting ISA descriptions as standalone data, making the validation engine resilient to hardware updates. Furthermore, the framework employs an analysis-driven validation mechanism that enables multi-stage validation, simplifying rule construction and enhancing extensibility. We demonstrate how SHARP supports hardware-specific validation tasks and discuss its impact on quantum software development, including language decoupling, program-level constraint validation, and feature access control. Our findings suggest that SHARP provides a path toward a scalable and maintainable programming interface for quantum computing.

papers.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
papers.authors: Teerawat Tongloy; Rangsan Jomtarak
papers.abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, the decomposition needs no approximation: each class's probability above its no-information share splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM) over the picture and measurable on the hardware that classifies. For the quadratic form behind each class probability it equals Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline, in closed form. Deleting the 5 % of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73 % to 9 %, as occlusion does with 1,024 extra runs per picture, whereas gradient saliency removes much less. One architecture serves both: a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at a single wavelength reach 72.3 % on Caltech-10 colour photographs (96.8 % on MNIST, 86.7 % on Fashion-MNIST, 47.9 % on colour CIFAR-10). On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask applied before approximate loading, 300 Caltech-10 test pictures were classified at 37.7 % against 10 % by chance (56.3 % in exact simulation), and 2x2 maps of ten correctly and confidently classified pictures, estimated on the chip, agreed with the exact ones (r = 0.77). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data.

papers.title: Quantum Path Finder: Navigating Constraint Space via Non-Abelian Gauge Dynamics
papers.authors: Chunyin Chen; Biao Wu
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms are commonly designed within the circuit paradigm or through adiabatic evolution. Here we introduce \emph{Quantum Path Finder} (QPF), a distinct algorithm-design paradigm based on non-Abelian gauge dynamics in a constraint-protected degenerate manifold. Each Boolean variable is promoted to a qutrit whose additional state represents an unassigned variable. The problem Hamiltonian then defines a connected manifold of feasible partial assignments, and time-dependent local qutrit rotations generate coherent transport on this manifold. Unlike conventional adiabatic quantum computation, QPF does not require the state to follow an instantaneous eigenstate along a prescribed interpolation: adiabaticity with respect to the constraint gap protects the feasible manifold, while adiabatic following within that manifold is optional. The algorithmic task is therefore to design paths and interference in constraint space rather than only to engineer a sequence of gates or a ground-state interpolation. We illustrate the framework with three applications. For unstructured search, a two-level analysis and numerical evolution recover Grover-type scaling under explicitly stated assumptions. For complete $3$-XORSAT, the accessible gauge sector has a size-independent gap, in contrast to the exponentially closing gap of a conventional transverse-field adiabatic path. For satisfiable $3$-SAT instances, finite-size benchmarks demonstrate high satisfied-clause fractions at short classical comparison budgets, without claiming an equal-cost quantum advantage. We also outline a superconducting-qutrit implementation and discuss the conceptual relationship between QPF and nondeterministic Turing machine.

papers.title: Experimental demonstration of phase-conjugated twin-wave coherent reception over 100 km with injection locking assisted phase stabilization
papers.authors: Zhenlin Zhao; Xingwen Yi; Dawei Wang
papers.abstract: Recovering complex optical signals with high sensitivity is central to coherent communication and sensing. Beyond conventional homodyne and heterodyne reception, phase-conjugate twin-wave encoding and phase-sensitive joint detection offer an alternative strategy with enhanced sensitivity. Extending this approach to long-distance transmission of high-order-modulated signals is challenging because optical phase coherence must be maintained at the receiver. Here we experimentally demonstrate injection-locking-assisted phase-conjugated twin-wave reception of 200-MBaud signals with modulation formats up to 256-QAM over 100 km of optical fiber. Optical injection locking regenerates the local oscillator (LO) from a reference transmitted through the 16 dB-loss link, while pilot-assisted optical feedback stabilizes the relative signal-LO phase, enabling coherent combining of the phase-conjugated twin waves at a single balanced photodetector. At equal received signal-photon number per quadrature in each data-carrying optical mode, the measured PCTW signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) exceeds the ideal single-mode homodyne standard quantum limit (SQL) benchmark. The SNR gains over the measured homodyne and conventional heterodyne results are about 3 dB and 6 dB, respectively. Constellation and bit-error-rate measurements show that this gain improves high-order data recovery relative to heterodyne reception. An ideal Gaussian-noise model predicts a photon information efficiency of 1.54 bits per received signal photon for uniform 16-QAM. These results establish an injection-locking-assisted coherent receiver architecture that implements joint detection of phase-conjugated twin waves over 100 km of fiber with enhanced sensitivity, providing a practical route for photon-efficient coherent communication.

papers.title: Tensor Contraction with ZX Calculus, a Graph-Theoretic Approach
papers.authors: Yuhao Han
papers.abstract: Tensors are higher dimensional generalisations of vectors and matrices. Tensor networks are a diagrammatic representation of complicated relations between tensors, and tensor contraction is the evaluation of a tensor network analogous to matrix multiplication. Tensor networks and tensor contraction are ubiquitous in computer science, physics, and applied mathematics. Most existing tensor contraction algorithms are focused on finding an optimal contraction order of the tensors' bonds. However, finding the optimal order is an NP-hard problem. It is equivalent to another possibly more straightforward but still NP-hard problem of finding the treewidth of the line graph of the tensor network. While in general finding the optimal bond-by-bond contraction order is hard, in many practical cases there is no need to find an optimal order. This observation leads to the core innovation of this thesis, which is a new tensor contraction paradigm that uses graph theoretic operations to produce an equivalent tensor network whose line graph has lower treewidth than the original tensor network, before applying the bond-by-bond contraction algorithm. We call these graph theoretical operations \textit{rewrite preprocessing}, and we name the algorithms that apply rewrite preprocessing before regular bond-by-bond contraction \textit{Tensor Contraction with Graph Operation}. There are many possible ways to perform rewrite preprocessing; in this thesis, we focus on the graph operations of ZX calculus, a diagrammatic language for quantum circuits. Ample numerical simulations have been performed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

papers.title: Long-term yields of short-rate models as Feynman-Kac ground states: a variational quantum eigensolver with single-setting energy estimation on two NISQ platforms
papers.authors: Doyeol "David" Ahn
papers.abstract: We show that the long-term yield of a short-rate model is the ground-state energy of a Schrodinger operator obtained from the Feynman-Kac bond-pricing equation, so that it can be computed by a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We treat the Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Black-Karasinski models; the last has no closed form. Calibrated monthly to the U.S. Treasury curve from 1985 to 2026, the long-term yield follows the 30-year yield with an in-sample correlation of 0.98. The Hamiltonian is stoquastic, so its ground state is positive and the energy can be estimated from computational-basis samples with a single measurement setting. On ibm_cleveland, gate noise appears mainly as bit flips of the high-order qubits. A bit-flip deconvolution with a tail set fixed by a WKB criterion, combined with readout mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation, gives four-qubit estimates within 33-125 bp of the grid ground-state energies for all three models, and within 23-67 bp for Treasury-calibrated parameters. On IonQ Forte Enterprise the same analysis reduces the error in the same proportions. On the same circuits, a Pauli-measurement VQE deviates by 791-1,129 bp, so the single-setting estimator gives about ten times smaller errors with one setting instead of nine. An on-device VQE converges from 4,939 bp to 130 bp.

papers.title: Quantum Recovery from Black-Hole Radiation Beyond the Emission Yield
papers.authors: Kashif Ammar Yasir
papers.abstract: A proposed resolution of the black-hole information paradox must explain which information an outside observer can recover from escaping radiation\cite{Hawking,Page,Hayden,Almheiri}. Environmental memory can return correlations to the source without delivering them to that observer\cite{ChenQi,ChenMemory}. Here we establish a sharp recovery frontier at fixed mean radiation yield for single-excitation channels and realize its qubit limit with an autonomous quantum-memory emitter. Unequal transmissions balance retained coherence against information in failed collection events. A reference--radiation correlation test distinguishes this gain even when the mean collected energy is unchanged. Identical transmission channels instead give the same recovery at matched collection, regardless of their emission timescales. For a broader class of interacting sources, an ordering of collected and inaccessible coupling spectra forbids unassisted quantum transmission irrespective of internal memory. A separate coding example supports a positive rate where uniform transmission at matched actual yield has zero capacity. Together, these results identify what openness must change to assist recovery: the accessible transmission structure. They supply a physically constrained comparison of evaporation mechanisms, separating information delivered to radiation from coherence retained elsewhere or an increase in the collected output.

papers.title: Quantum Lower Bounds for Collision Problems
papers.authors: Pan Peng; Jingyu Wu
papers.abstract: We establish tight lower bounds on the adaptive and non-adaptive quantum query complexities of Promised $k$-to-one Finding on an exactly $k$-to-one input string $x\in\mathbb Z_q^n$, for every fixed $k\ge2$ and every feasible alphabet size $q\ge n/k$. The lower bounds are $Ω_k(n^{1/2-1/(2(2^k-1))})$ for unrestricted adaptive algorithms and $Ω_k(n^{1-1/k})$ for one-round non-adaptive algorithms. The former matches the adaptive quantum algorithm of Liu and Zhandry [LZ19], whereas the latter matches classical birthday sampling even when the parallel queries are arbitrarily entangled. We also establish the non-adaptive lower bound $Ω_k(\sqrt{n/k})$ for $k$-to-one Testing when $q\ge n$, resolving an open question posed by Koiran, Landes, Portier, and Yao [KLPY10]. Our proofs generate the balanced input from a uniformly random permutation and use compressed permutation oracles to describe the information learned by the algorithm. The adaptive proof bounds the growth of partial collisions through successive queries. The one-round proof instead analyzes the state after the parallel queries directly, bounding the probability that the compressed database contains a full collision. In both proofs, a short verification step accounts for correct outputs that include unrecorded positions. For the decision problem, we also compare one-round states with independent and distinct output labels.

papers.title: An Observable-Algebra Approach to Quantum Coherence in Anyonic Systems
papers.authors: Cheng-Qian Xu; D. L. Zhou
papers.abstract: Physical restrictions on operations can make quantum coherence inaccessible. Quantifying off-diagonal density matrix elements in a chosen basis alone does not reveal which information is hidden by each restriction. To distinguish their effects, we describe physical restrictions through subalgebras of accessible observables. The associated trace-preserving conditional expectations unify two reconstruction principles: each gives both the maximum-entropy state compatible with the accessible data and the closest state in the corresponding subalgebra in relative entropy. We apply this framework to anyonic systems to separate the contributions from local-charge superselection and non-Abelian fusion rules. We prove that the charge-line severing map is the conditional expectation onto the local-product subalgebra. It is completely positive and quantum-trace-preserving, and uniquely reconstructs a state in this space from all local-product expectation values. The hierarchy of measurement restrictions then separates total bipartite coherence into three nonnegative contributions: coherence between local charges, inaccessible fusion information, and conventional coherence. The first two decompose the anyonic charge entanglement and distinguish the effects of local-charge superselection from the remaining fusion information. Finally, we relate basis-independent measures of anyonic coherence to entanglement. For pure anyonic states with vacuum total charge, the optimized total and correlated coherence equal the total and conventional relative-entropy entanglement, respectively.

papers.title: Quantum-enhanced multiphase estimation with spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates
papers.authors: Jiaheng Jin; Xinwei Li; Dong E. Liu; Li You
papers.abstract: We investigate quantum-enhanced two-phase estimation in a spin-$1$ Bose-Einstein condensate, where spin-exchange collisions generate a spin-nematic squeezed state in the $m_F=\pm1$ modes. The resulting pair-correlated state has a rank-one quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) for the two mode phases relative to the $m_F=0$ mode and therefore cannot resolve them independently. Nevertheless, we find that a parameter-independent passive three-mode transformation lifts this rank deficiency and enables joint estimation of both phases. In the undepleted-pump regime, we derive expressions for the QFIM, optimize the equal-weight multiparameter quantum Cramér-Rao bound, and obtain a full-rank probe with squeezing-enhanced sensitivity below the matched fixed-total-number standard quantum limit (SQL). These analytical predictions are confirmed by exact-diagonalization calculations. We further construct a parameter-independent readout that maps the phase combinations onto displacement channels accessible through atomic homodyne or parity measurements. Our results provide a route from spin-mixing-generated quantum correlations to two-phase estimation in spinor condensates.

papers.title: Mitigating sloppiness with intermediate controls in sequential multiparameter spin interferometry
papers.authors: Hai Feng; Xinwei Li; Rong Lu; Li You
papers.abstract: Multiparameter quantum sensing requires different parameters to produce distinguishable probe responses while allowing their information to be extracted simultaneously. In sequential sensing without intermediate control, two phases encoded through the same generator are locally indistinguishable. Here we show that parameter-independent intermediate controls overcome this limitation in a collective-spin interferometer by separating the corresponding effective generators in the probe covariance geometry. Specifically, a transverse collective rotation provides an analytically tractable realization, and intermediate one-axis twisting (OAT) generates additional nonlinear operator directions and a broad regime of enhanced joint estimation. For fixed total particle number $N$ and matched twisting resource, both marginal precision bounds lie below those of a separated-OAT strategy while measurement incompatibility remains weak. For intermediate OAT, conditional optimization of an upper bound on the Holevo cost yields asymptotic $N^{-2}$ scaling. For this protocol, a fixed rotated-Dicke measurement retains simultaneous two-parameter enhancement over a broad phase region. These results show that nonlinear intermediate control can mitigate sloppiness while preserving quantum-enhanced precision with a common readout.

papers.title: Decoherence suppression in quantum dense coding
papers.authors: Xi Yan; Wen-Jie Zhang; Jun-Hong An
papers.abstract: By harnessing entanglement to transmit information beyond the limits of classical communication, quantum dense coding serves as a key component in various quantum technologies. However, in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, noise-induced decoherence poses inevitable challenges to its practical implementation. By investigating the non-Markovian decoherence dynamics of the two categories of quantum dense coding protocols realized in discrete- and continuous-variable systems, we demonstrate a physical mechanism to suppress the decoherence in quantum dense coding. It is found that the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum of the entire system consisting of each subsystem and its local environment of the quantum channel restores the quantum advantage of dense coding in the presence of decoherence. Refreshing our understanding on the noisy effect on quantum dense coding, our finding offers a guide toward the practical realization of noise-tolerant quantum dense coding.

papers.title: Bounds and sufficient conditions in quantum Zeno effect
papers.authors: Vladimir Parfenyev; Sergey Belan
papers.abstract: When a quantum system undergoes a series of repeated measurements during its time evolution to check whether it remains in the initial state, the resulting state lifetime can decrease (the quantum Zeno effect) or increase (the quantum inverse Zeno effect) as the inter-measurement period increases. Several transitions between these two regimes may occur within the same system. A carefully chosen measurement period $τ_\ast$ (or rate $r_\ast$ in the case of a stochastic measurement protocol) brings the state lifetime to its global minimum. Here, we describe the upper and lower bounds on the optimized state lifetime, which are expressed in terms of characteristic time scales encoded in the state survival probability $P(T)$, which is assumed to decrease monotonically to zero at large $T$. In addition, we analyze the bounds on the optimal measurement periods/rates and formulate sufficient conditions for observing the inverse Zeno effect. The analysis is also extended to states with non-monotonic survival functions. The results are illustrated numerically with an example of a system of optically trapped ultra-cold atoms.

papers.title: Access Resources and Stability of Error-Correction Capabilities in Continuous Strategic Codes
papers.authors: He Wang
papers.abstract: Continuous quantum error correction depends on which parts of a measurement record remain available to the controller at recovery. We study this temporal access using continuous strategic codes, formulated as open continuous process tensors contracted with causal instruments and conditional recovery. For monitored stabilizer codes, a common-optimal-correction criterion identifies when records can be merged without loss and yields a factorization for separated CSS inference. Terminal decision labels and causal persistent memory carry different costs: five persistent classical states reach the complete-record optimum in a finite-strength counting model, whereas its two-window diffusive counterpart has nine terminal decision labels and requires unbounded memory for exact causal recovery. Uniform lower and constructive upper bounds establish an optimal fidelity deficit of order $m^{-2}$ for $m$ persistent states in the diffusive model. Counting and diffusive stability bounds translate open-process approximation into guarantees for deployed-controller performance and retained access advantages, quantified by explicit quantizers and model-mismatch curves. The same process--instrument framework connects storage with persistent environments and irreversible noise to spacetime interrogation and record-selected paths for a logical $T$ gate. These results specify which record distinctions recovery needs, the memory cost of approximating them, and the logical protection retained under model error.

papers.title: From Ghost SICs to SIC-POVMs: A Galois Reduction of Zauner's Conjecture
papers.authors: Hassan Khodaiemehr
papers.abstract: Symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (SIC-POVMs, or SICs) are optimal minimal measurements for quantum state tomography. Problem~1 of Horodecki, Rudnicki and Życzkowski's open problems in quantum information asks for SICs in infinitely many dimensions. By work of Appleby--Flammia--Kopp and Radchenko--Wheeler, ghost SICs, which satisfy the SIC equations with Hermiticity up to parity, exist unconditionally for $d\ge4$. We study the passage from ghosts to SICs. We compute all isolated points of the complexified SIC variety for $d=4,5,6$; exactly half are SICs. We prove that no symmetry of the SIC equations maps a ghost to a SIC, so the step is purely arithmetic, and that a SIC exists in dimension $d$ whenever the ghost overlap units satisfy a place law: each Galois conjugate is real or unimodular according to the infinite place of the real quadratic field $F$ below it. If the unit field is abelian over $F$, the place law is the Stark relation $c_-=κ$; equivalently, a Galois conjugate of an associated near-group fusion category is unitary exactly when it is pseudo-unitary. For $d$ a power of a prime $p\equiv5\pmod 6$ or of $3$, an infinite family, we prove that under the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture $c_-=κ$ is equivalent to the triviality of $κ$ on the Hilbert-class-field part of the unit field. That condition involves no complex conjugation, and it follows from a sign-free multiplet hypothesis. We state an explicit $GL_2$ reciprocity law for the squared ghost overlaps that implies $c_-=κ$, and we prove it for the computed algebraic overlaps in $d=5,7,11,15$ by Artin reciprocity and a check in every ray class. Zauner's conjecture remains open: the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture and the multiplet hypothesis are not proved here.
